infoIntroH2: What is a kiln loading calculator?
infoIntroP: The Kiln Loading Calculator works out how many pieces you can fit into a kiln for one firing before you start loading. First, it calculates how many pieces fit across a single shelf (or "bat") — width and depth divided by piece size after subtracting the gap between pieces and the margin around the shelf's edge. Then it calculates how many shelf layers fit within the kiln's height, based on piece height plus shelf thickness plus the clearance needed above each shelf for even heat circulation. Multiplying these two numbers gives you the total number of pieces that fit in the kiln at once.
infoHowtoP: Enter your kiln's interior size (width, depth, height) and your shelf size (width, depth, thickness). Choose whether your pieces are round, square, or rectangular, then enter the diameter (round), side length (square), or width and depth (rectangular), plus height. The gap between pieces, the shelf edge margin, and the clearance above each shelf all come pre-filled with commonly used defaults — adjust them only if you need to. Once everything's entered, pieces per shelf, shelves needed, and total firing capacity are calculated instantly, along with a diagram.

deepDiveH2: Why might more pieces actually fit than the calculated number?
deepDiveP: This calculator uses a grid layout — pieces arranged in straight rows and columns. In real-world practice, though, potters sometimes use a staggered, hexagonal packing arrangement instead, which can fit up to about 15% more round pieces into the same area (because circles pack more densely in a hexagonal arrangement than in a square grid). So the number this calculator gives you is a safe lower bound — "you can definitely fit at least this many" — and with clever arranging, the real number may come out higher.
deepDiveListH2: Good to know when planning a kiln load
deepDiveList: When placing multiple shelves side by side in one layer, don't forget the gaps between shelves also eat into usable space — the more shelves per layer, the more that adds up
If your pieces vary in height, the layer spacing needs to accommodate the tallest one — grouping similar-height pieces onto the same layer uses space more efficiently
Temperature can vary slightly near the kiln walls, so many potters prefer keeping their most important pieces toward the center — a generous edge margin naturally builds that buffer in
If you're accounting for firing shrinkage when calculating clearance, remember to enter the pre-fired (greenware) piece size into this tool, not the expected fired size

faq.q: Is the calculation accurate for round pieces too?
faq.a: Round pieces are conservatively fit into square cells sized to their diameter. In practice, staggered (hexagonal) arrangements can fit slightly more, but this calculator gives you a safe minimum estimate.

faq.q: Why do I need clearance above the shelf?
faq.a: It's standard practice to leave some space between a piece and the shelf above it so heat can circulate evenly during firing. Accounting for this clearance is what makes the layer count accurate.

faq.q: Could more pieces actually fit than the calculated number?
faq.a: Yes. This calculator is an approximation based on a grid layout, so depending on piece shape and how you actually arrange them, more may fit than the calculated value.

faq.q: If the kiln and shelf are the same size, can I leave the margin at 0?
faq.a: Unless the shelf fits the kiln's interior walls with zero tolerance, we'd recommend leaving some margin. Setting it to 0 removes any allowance for real-world construction variance or the clearance needed to slide the shelf in and out.

faq.q: Can this calculate a kiln load with mixed piece sizes?
faq.a: This tool calculates for one piece size at a time. If you're planning to fire mixed sizes, we'd suggest grouping pieces by size and running the calculation separately for each group.

faq.q: When would I set boards per layer higher than 1?
faq.a: That's for larger kilns where the floor is too wide for a single shelf to cover, so multiple shelves need to sit side by side. Smaller kilns usually only need 1.

privacyNote: This tool performs all calculations entirely in your browser. Nothing you enter is sent to or stored on a server.
